title: The Fourier Transform
intro: The Fourier transform describes a signal by the sinusoids it is made of: how much of each frequency, and where each one starts. This topic builds signals out of sinusoids in a 3D view, follows the idea from repeating waves to single pulses and sampled data, and ends with the fast Fourier transform, the algorithm that made all of it practical.

blocks.text: A sound, a radio signal or a row of pixels can be written down in two ways. One is by time (or position): its value at each moment. The other is by frequency: how much of each sinusoid you would have to add up to build it. The Fourier transform goes from the first to the second, and the inverse transform comes back:

blocks.tex: X(f) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x(t)\, e^{-j2\pi f t}\, dt, \qquad x(t) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} X(f)\, e^{j2\pi f t}\, df

blocks.text: $X(f)$ is a complex number for every frequency $f$ in hertz: its size $|X(f)|$ says how much of that frequency the signal holds, and its angle says where that sinusoid starts (its phase). Nothing is lost going either way. The same signal is simply being described in a different language.

For a signal that repeats with period $T$ the recipe is simpler: only the frequencies $0, 1/T, 2/T, \ldots$ appear, and the signal is a sum of those harmonics, its Fourier series. The viewer below shows that sum spread out in 3D.

Time runs across the 3D view, frequency runs into it, and height is the value. Each harmonic is a coloured ribbon standing at its own frequency; in front, the dark curve is their sum and the dashed curve is the signal itself; on the right-hand wall, a bar for each harmonic shows its amplitude. Looked at from the front, the ribbons add up to the signal: the time domain. Turned to look along the time axis, only the bars are left: the frequency domain. Pick a signal, then press Next step ▶ to walk through it in eight steps.

items: Drag the 3D view to turn it, or use Turn and Tilt. Steps 4 and 5 of the walk-through turn it for you, to the front and to the side.
Harmonics added, N, sets how many harmonics are summed (k = 0 to N). Add harmonics plays N upward from 0 so you can watch the sum close in on the signal.
Period T stretches the signal in time. The harmonics sit at k/T hertz, so a longer period packs them closer together on the spectrum panel's fixed 0 to 10 Hz axis.
Delay slides the signal to the right by a fraction of a period. The amplitudes do not change; every phase in the right-hand panel moves.
The middle panel is the amplitude spectrum: a stem at each frequency k/T as tall as $A_k$. Hollow stems are harmonics that exist but are not added yet.

blocks.text: The picture is the Fourier series of a repeating signal. A single pulse that never repeats has a continuous spectrum, every frequency rather than a comb of harmonics; the From Series to Transform (#/math/fourier-transform/series-to-transform) page gets there by letting the period grow.

items: Sinusoids and Complex Exponentials (#/math/fourier-transform/sinusoids): amplitude, frequency and phase, and why $e^{j\omega t}$, a turning arrow, is the simplest way to handle all three.
Fourier Series: Building a Wave (#/math/fourier-transform/fourier-series): the coefficient integral, why it works (orthogonality), and the square, sawtooth and triangle waves worked out.
Reading a Spectrum (#/math/fourier-transform/spectrum): amplitude and phase spectra, one-sided and two-sided, and Parseval's theorem: energy counted either way.
Convergence and the Gibbs Phenomenon (#/math/fourier-transform/convergence): how fast the coefficients fall, why jumps converge slowly, and the 9% overshoot that never goes away.
From Series to Transform (#/math/fourier-transform/series-to-transform): stretching the period to infinity, the Fourier transform of a pulse, a table of pairs, and the link to the Laplace transform.

Properties of the Transform (#/math/fourier-transform/properties): shifts, scaling, modulation, convolution, and the uncertainty principle: a signal cannot be short in time and narrow in frequency at once.
Sampling and the DFT (#/math/fourier-transform/sampling-and-dft): sampling, aliasing and the Nyquist rate, the discrete Fourier transform, leakage and windows.
The Fast Fourier Transform (#/math/fourier-transform/fft): how splitting a DFT into even and odd samples cuts $N^2$ work to $N\log_2 N$, with a butterfly diagram to step through.
A Gallery of Waves (#/math/fourier-transform/gallery): every signal in the viewer, walked through from waveform to spectrum.
Fourier Transform Tables (#/math/fourier-transform/tables): the Fourier family, pairs and properties to look up.

blocks.text: Sines and cosines, Euler's formula $e^{j\theta} = \cos\theta + j\sin\theta$, and what an integral means. This topic writes the imaginary unit as $j$, as engineers do. The library's page Complex Numbers for Quantum Mechanics (#/quantum/foundations/complex-numbers) covers the polar form, and Integrals (#/math/calculus/integrals) covers integration. The Fourier transform is the Laplace transform (The Laplace Transform (#/math/laplace-transform)) taken on the imaginary axis, when that axis lies in its region of convergence; you do not need that topic first, but the two light each other up.

A note on conventions: this topic writes the transform with frequency $f$ in hertz, $e^{-j2\pi ft}$, which puts no $2\pi$ in front of either integral. Many books use angular frequency $\omega = 2\pi f$ instead, and then a $1/2\pi$ appears in the inverse. The two describe the same thing: $X(\omega)$ in those books is $X(f)$ here at $f = \omega/2\pi$.
